prompt: A newly inserted node in a Red-Black tree is coloured red. Which of the four rules is it most likely to violate?
options: Rule 1 — every node is red or black
Rule 2 — the root is black
Rule 3 — a red node never has a red child
Rule 4 — every path to a nil leaf contains the same number of black nodes
explanation: Colouring the new node red deliberately preserves rule 4 (the black-height is unchanged). The price is rule 3: if the new node's parent is also red, a red-red pair appears and the fixup routine is triggered. (Rule 2 is only violated in the special case where the new node *is* the root, which is fixed by a single recolouring.)

prompt: The Red-Black tree rules — which two statements are correct?
options: Every path from a node to any of its descendant nil leaves contains the same number of black nodes.
If a node has exactly one real child, that child must be red.
Every path from the root to a nil leaf contains the same number of *red* nodes.
Both children of a red node must be red.
explanation: The black-height rule ✓ directly implies the single-child consequence: a black single child would make that side's black count higher than the missing side's ✓. Red nodes are unconstrained in *count* per path ✗, and rule 3 says the opposite of option 4 — a red node's children must be black ✗.

prompt: Height and complexity of Red-Black trees — which two statements are correct?
options: The four rules guarantee a height of at most 2·log(n+1).
Search, insert and delete are all Θ(log n) in the worst case.
A Red-Black tree's height bound is tighter than an AVL tree's.
Rebalancing after an insert may require Θ(log n) rotations.
explanation: The ≤ 2·log(n+1) bound ✓ is exactly what makes all three operations Θ(log n) in the worst case ✓. AVL's ≈1.44·log(n+2) bound is *tighter*, not looser ✗. Insert fixup needs at most 2 rotations (the recolouring may propagate up, but rotations do not) ✗.

prompt: Red-Black insert and delete — which two statements are correct?
options: Insert fixup needs at most two rotations, however far the recolouring propagates upward.
Delete can create a "double black" deficiency, which the delete-fixup resolves in one of four standard cases.
Delete never needs a rotation, since only colours have to be repaired.
Insert fixup starts at the root and works downward.
explanation: Two rotations always suffice for insert ✓, and removing a black node produces the double-black deficiency handled by the four sibling cases ✓. Those cases include rotations ✗, and both fixups walk *upward* from the modified node ✗.

prompt: The T.nil sentinel in Red-Black tree implementations — which two statements are correct?
options: A single shared sentinel node, coloured black, replaces all nil pointers.
It removes almost all null-pointer special cases from insert and delete.
Each nil leaf needs its own separate sentinel object.
The sentinel is coloured red so that it never affects the black-height.
explanation: One shared black sentinel ✓ gives every node valid left/right/parent references, eliminating the null checks ✓. Sharing a single object is the whole point — per-leaf sentinels would waste Θ(n) memory ✗ — and it must be *black* so the black-height rule counts consistently ✗.

prompt: Rotations as a rebalancing primitive — which two statements are correct?
options: A rotation is a local O(1) restructuring that changes which of two adjacent nodes is on top.
A rotation preserves the in-order sequence of the keys, hence the BST property.
A rotation changes the in-order sequence, which is why the keys must be re-sorted afterwards.
rotateLeft and rotateRight each cost Θ(log n), since the subtree heights must be recomputed.
explanation: A rotation relinks a constant number of pointers ✓ and is specifically designed to leave the in-order order untouched ✓ — that is what makes it safe for BSTs, AVL and RB trees alike. Options 3 and 4 contradict both facts ✗✗ (only the two rotated nodes' heights need updating, which is O(1)).
